title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: There is no future tense to learn. M4's non-past is unmarked for time, and sa- glued to its front aims it at the future: adhhab (I go, I am going) becomes sa-adhhab (I will go). Nothing inside the verb moves.
sa- never changes for person — the person stays in the prefix underneath it: sa-adhhab (I), sa-tadhhab (you-m, she), sa-yadhhab (he), sa-nadhhab (we). After M5's four suffixes, this is a rest.

sawfa says the same thing as a free word standing in front of the verb, and lands a little heavier — closer to "I shall" than to "I'll". sa- does the everyday work; sawfa is worth recognising and using sparingly.

English needs an auxiliary — "will go", "am going to go" — and Arabic has none to borrow: the marker is welded to the verb. Use ONE of sa- and sawfa, never both. *sawfa sa-adhhab is the English habit wearing two hats.
A future time word on its own is often enough: ghadan ākul fī al-bayt is good Arabic with no sa- in it at all. Arabic marks the future once and lets it stand; English repeats "will" in every clause.

ghadan and qarīban keep their -an. It is the adverbial ending this course writes (with shukran, kathīran, dāʾiman, aḥyānan), not a case ending. As the adverb the word is ghadan and never *ghad: the bare noun ghad exists ("the morrow") but it is not what goes in these sentences.
Not every time phrase wears -an. al-usbūʿ al-qādim ("the coming week") and baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr ("after the noon") are ordinary noun phrases doing adverbial work, exactly like M4's al-yawm.

kāna comes back a third time. The present has no verb at all (al-jaww bārid), the past has kāna (kāna al-jaww bārid ams), and the future has sa-yakūn (sa-yakūn al-jaww bārid ghadan). Two tenses out of three need the verb M1 said was missing.
The question is M2's hal in front and nothing else moves: hal sa-tadhhab ilā as-sūq ghadan? English has to turn "you will" into "will you"; Arabic leaves the sentence exactly as it stood.
Bounded on purpose: no future negation in L1. MSA needs lan plus a verb shape this level does not teach, so this module stays affirmative, questions aside.

in shāʾ Allāh ("God willing") is attached to almost every plan in real speech, by speakers of every background, and sits closer to English "hopefully" than to a statement of faith. Learn it as the tail of a plan, not as a separate subject.

sentences.cue: I will go to school tomorrow

words.note: sa- is the whole future: a single letter glued to the front of M4's adhhab, and the verb underneath is untouched. It never changes for person — the person is still the prefix beneath it: sa-adhhab (I), sa-tadhhab (you-m or she), sa-yadhhab (he), sa-nadhhab (we) — and to a woman, M3's -īn tail rides through the future untouched: sa-tadhhabīn. It is not a word and cannot stand alone.

"Tomorrow", standing free at either end of the sentence like M5's ams. The -an is the adverbial ending this course writes, as in shukran and dāʾiman — as the adverb it is always ghadan, so never trim it to *ghad.

sentences.trap: sa- is not a word. It cannot be moved, spaced off the verb, or said on its own — it lives on the front of the verb the way al- lives on the front of a noun.
sentences.sound: sa-ADH-hab i-LAA al-MAD-ra-sa GHA-dan — the sa- is quick and unstressed, and the verb keeps the beat it had in M4.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will go to school
variations.changed: ghadan takes the front seat — either end is fine, as with ams

variations.cue: He will go to school tomorrow
variations.changed: sa- holds still and the prefix underneath turns from a- to ya-: he

variations.cue: You will go to school tomorrow (to a woman)
variations.changed: sa- holds still and the -īn tail rides through the future: sa-tadhhabīn

mistake.why: sa- written off on its own, as if it were a word like English "will". It is a prefix: it is written joined, and only sawfa can stand apart.

sentences.usage: The plainest plan there is — where you are going tomorrow.
sentences.mnemonic: sa- = "soon": one letter on the front of the verb and you are in tomorrow.

sentences.cue: I will go to work tomorrow

words.note: The other future marker, and the only one that is a word of its own: it stands in front of the verb with a space, where sa- is glued on. Same meaning, a heavier tread — sawfa is the "I shall" of the pair, and sa- is what people say all day.

sentences.trap: One marker, not two. sawfa and sa- do the same job, so *sawfa sa-adhhab doubles a marker English would only have said once.
sentences.sound: SAW-fa ADH-hab i-LAA al-ʿA-mal GHA-dan — sawfa is its own word and takes its own stress.

variations.cue: I will go to work tomorrow
variations.changed: sawfa → sa-: the everyday version of the same sentence

variations.cue: We will go to work
variations.changed: the person is still in the verb, not in sawfa: na- is we

variations.cue: He will go to work
variations.changed: sawfa stands its ground and the prefix underneath turns to ya-: he

mistake.why: Both markers at once. sawfa and sa- are two spellings of the same future, so a sentence takes one or the other — sawfa adhhab, or sa-adhhab.

sentences.usage: A plan stated with a little weight — an announcement rather than a remark.
sentences.mnemonic: sawfa is the long one, so it sounds like the long promise.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I will drink a coffee in the morning

words.note: M3's ashrab with the same sa- on its front, and the same four persons underneath: sa-ashrab (I), sa-tashrab (you-m or she), sa-yashrab (he), sa-nashrab (we). One prefix serves every verb in the language — nothing here is special to drinking.

sentences.trap: The time words you learned for habits work for plans unchanged: fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ is still "in the morning", and it is sa- alone that decides which morning.
sentences.sound: GHA-dan sa-ASH-rab QAH-wa fi ṣ-ṣa-BAAḤ — said, the fī melts into the article.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will drink the tea in the evening
variations.changed: swap drink and time — the frame does not move

variations.cue: Tomorrow she will drink a coffee in the morning
variations.changed: ta- underneath the sa-: you (to a man), or she

variations.cue: Will you drink a coffee tomorrow? (to a man)
variations.changed: hal in front and the plan is a question — nothing else moves

mistake.why: M5's past verb under a future time word. ghadan needs the non-past, with or without sa-: sa-ashrab. sharibtu belongs to ams.

sentences.usage: Saying what tomorrow's morning holds — the small plans a day is made of.
sentences.mnemonic: sa-ashrab: the same ashrab, one letter later.

sentences.display: hal sa-tadhhab ilā as-sūq baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr?
sentences.script: هل ستذهب إلى السوق بعد الظهر؟
sentences.cue: Will you go to the market this afternoon? (to a man)
sentences.glossEn: lit. "question will-you-go to the-market after the-noon"
sentences.literal: Q will-go-you to the-market after the-noon

words.note: Literally "after the noon", and learned whole like M4's fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ. ẓ is a sun letter, so the article assimilates and is written as it is said: aẓ-ẓuhr, never *al-ẓuhr. ẓuhr on its own is noon, the middle of the day.

sentences.trap: "Will you…?" reorders English and reorders nothing in Arabic: hal goes in front of the sentence you already had, and sa-tadhhab keeps its seat.
sentences.sound: hal sa-TADH-hab i-LAA as-SOOQ BAʿD aẓ-ẒUHR — the ẓ is heavy and the two of them run together as one long sound.

variations.display: hal sa-tadhhabīn ilā as-sūq baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr?
variations.script: هل ستذهبين إلى السوق بعد الظهر؟
variations.cue: Will you go to the market this afternoon? (to a woman)
variations.changed: the -īn ending, as in M3's turīdīn: the question turns to a woman

variations.cue: Yes, I will go in the afternoon
variations.changed: the answer: ta- turns back to a-, I

variations.cue: No, I will go tomorrow
variations.changed: the other answer: lā stands alone, and the plan simply moves — no verb is negated

mistake.display: hal sa-tadhhab ilā as-sūq baʿd al-ẓuhr?
mistake.script: هل ستذهب إلى السوق بعد الظهر؟
mistake.why: al-ẓuhr is not another spelling of aẓ-ẓuhr — it is no word at all. ẓ is a sun letter, and this course writes the assimilation, exactly as it writes ash-shāy and aṣ-ṣabāḥ. Bare Arabic script writes neither spelling differently, which is precisely why the romanization has to.

sentences.usage: Making an arrangement for later the same day.
sentences.mnemonic: baʿd aẓ-ẓuhr — after the ẓuhr, the noon everything else is measured from.

sentences.display: ghadan ākul fī al-bayt, in shāʾ Allāh
sentences.script: غدًا آكل في البيت، إن شاء الله
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'll eat at home, God willing
sentences.glossEn: lit. "tomorrow I-eat in the-house, if willed God"
sentences.literal: tomorrow eat-I in the-house, if willed God

words.note: Three words said as one, and attached to almost every plan in real speech by speakers of every background. It works the way English "hopefully" or "all being well" works: it softens a promise rather than making a religious claim. The medial hamza of shāʾ is written; Allāh keeps its long ā.

sentences.trap: No sa- here, and the sentence is still about tomorrow: ghadan alone is enough. Arabic marks the future once — English cannot resist a second "will".
sentences.sound: GHA-dan AA-kul fi l-BAYT, in SHAAʾ al-LAAH — said fast it runs together as inshaʾAllāh, one word.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I will eat at home
variations.changed: add sa- — the same plan, marked twice over

variations.display: sa-adhhab ilā as-sūq, in shāʾ Allāh
variations.script: سأذهب إلى السوق، إن شاء الله
variations.cue: I'll go to the market, God willing
variations.changed: the tail travels: any plan can take it

variations.display: ghadan yaʾkul fī al-bayt, in shāʾ Allāh
variations.script: غدًا يأكل في البيت، إن شاء الله
variations.cue: Tomorrow he'll eat at home, God willing
variations.changed: ya- and still no sa-: his plan, carried by ghadan alone — and the tail still softens it

mistake.why: ghadan cannot sit over a past verb. Without sa- the verb must still be the non-past: ghadan ākul. akaltu is yesterday's word.

sentences.usage: An everyday plan, held lightly — which is what in shāʾ Allāh is for.
sentences.mnemonic: in shāʾ Allāh — "if it is willed": the Arabic full stop on any plan.

sentences.cue: The weather will be cold tomorrow

words.cue: it will be, he will be
words.note: M5's kāna in the non-past, with sa- on the front: sa-akūn (I will be), sa-takūn (you-m or she), sa-yakūn (he or it), sa-nakūn (we). The bare yakūn is the same verb without the future marker. So "to be" is missing only from the present: the past needs kāna and the future needs yakūn.

sentences.trap: The three tenses of "to be" are not three verbs: al-jaww bārid (no verb) · kāna al-jaww bārid (past) · sa-yakūn al-jaww bārid (future). Only the present does without.
sentences.sound: sa-ya-KOON al-JAWW BAA-rid GHA-dan — jaww ends on a held, doubled w.

variations.cue: The weather was cold yesterday
variations.changed: back to M5's past — same frame, different end of the verb

variations.cue: The weather is cold today
variations.changed: the present, and the verb vanishes altogether

variations.cue: Will the weather be cold tomorrow?
variations.changed: hal + the forecast: will it be — the sentence behind it stands still

mistake.why: The verbless sentence is the PRESENT only. Tomorrow needs the verb back: sa-yakūn al-jaww bārid ghadan — the same lesson M5 taught with kāna, one tense further on.

sentences.usage: Weather talk about tomorrow — the sentence a forecast is made of.
sentences.mnemonic: kāna went, yakūn is coming: same three letters k-w-n, either side of now.

sentences.cue: I will be busy tomorrow (said by a man)

words.note: "Busy" — mashghūl of a man, mashghūla of a woman, agreeing with the SUBJECT like every adjective since ṭālib/ṭāliba. Full MSA would put an accusative ending on it after kāna or yakūn; this course's pause forms drop it, exactly as M5 did with kuntu taʿbān.

sentences.trap: Excusing yourself from tomorrow needs the verb. anā mashghūl is today; sa-akūn mashghūl is tomorrow.
sentences.sound: sa-a-KOON mash-GHOOL GHA-dan — the gh is a gargled g, the same letter as in ghadan.

variations.cue: I will be busy tomorrow (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a: the adjective follows the person it describes

variations.cue: You will be busy this afternoon (to a man)
variations.changed: ya- → ta-: the same future, aimed at you

variations.cue: Will you be busy tomorrow? (to a man)
variations.changed: the excuse asked for in advance: hal + sa-takūn, and mashghūl stays bare

mistake.why: sa- points at time that has not happened yet, and ams is over. Yesterday takes M5's verb: kuntu mashghūl ams — kāna for what was, sa-yakūn for what will be.

sentences.usage: Turning down an invitation for tomorrow, politely and without excuses.
sentences.mnemonic: mashghūl — "much-ghoul": too taken up to come out.

sentences.cue: I will go to the market next week

words.note: usbūʿ is a week and qādim is "coming", and the two are M3's noun-plus-adjective pattern with both halves carrying al-: al-usbūʿ al-qādim, "the week, the coming one". It wears no -an — it is an ordinary noun phrase put to adverbial work, exactly like M4's al-yawm.

sentences.trap: Both words take al-, because M3's law is still running: a definite noun takes a definite adjective. Drop one article and you have said "a week is the coming one".
sentences.sound: sa-ADH-hab i-LAA as-SOOQ al-us-BOOʿ al-QAA-dim — the ʿ closes usbūʿ off in the throat.

variations.cue: I will go to India next week
variations.changed: swap the destination — the time phrase holds

variations.cue: Next week I will go to the market
variations.changed: the time phrase takes the front seat, like ghadan

variations.cue: We will go to the market next week
variations.changed: a- → na- under the sa-: the plan becomes ours

mistake.why: With only one article this is a whole sentence — "the week is coming" — sitting inside another one. Both words need al- for the pair to be a phrase: al-usbūʿ al-qādim. That is M3's definiteness agreement, doing real work.

sentences.usage: Plans further out than tomorrow — the next step up from ghadan.
sentences.mnemonic: al-qādim — what is coming; qadam is a step, and next week is one step on.

sentences.cue: Soon I will go to India

words.note: "Soon", from qarīb (near) — nearness in time rather than in space. Another adverb wearing the written -an, beside ghadan, dāʾiman and aḥyānan; it sits at either end of the sentence.

sentences.trap: qarīban is vaguer than ghadan and just as future: with no sa- at all, qarīban adhhab ilā al-Hind would still be a plan.
sentences.sound: qa-REE-ban sa-ADH-hab i-LAA al-HIND — the q comes from the very back of the throat, as in as-sūq.

variations.cue: I will go to India soon
variations.changed: qarīban to the end — either seat is fine

variations.cue: Soon we will go to India
variations.changed: na- underneath the sa-: we

variations.cue: I shall go to India soon
variations.changed: sa- → sawfa: the free-standing marker, a shade heavier — one of the two, never both

mistake.why: qarīb is the adjective "near" and describes a thing — M7 teaches it as a word of its own. The adverb "soon" is qarīban, with the -an this course writes. Same word, one ending apart, two different jobs.

sentences.usage: A plan with no date on it yet — the honest answer to "when are you going?".
sentences.mnemonic: qarīban — "nearby" in time: near enough to say, not near enough to date.

sentences.display: ghadan sa-ākul al-khubz wa sa-ashrab al-ḥalīb
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I will eat the bread and drink the milk
sentences.glossEn: lit. "tomorrow will-I-eat the-bread and will-I-drink the-milk"
sentences.literal: tomorrow will-eat-I the-bread and will-drink-I the-milk

words.note: M4's ākul with sa- in front. The long ā of ākul is the I-prefix and the hamza hides inside it; the other persons put the hamza back on the page — sa-taʾkul (you-m or she), sa-yaʾkul (he). Written joined, one word, as every sa- verb is.

sentences.trap: Each verb carries its own sa-, the way M5's verbs each carried their own -tu. English says "will" once and lets it cover both halves.
sentences.sound: GHA-dan SAA-kul al-KHUBZ wa sa-ASH-rab al-ḥa-LEEB — sa-ākul runs into one long aa.

variations.display: ghadan sa-ākul al-fākiha wa sa-ashrab al-māʾ
variations.cue: Tomorrow I will eat the fruit and drink the water
variations.changed: swap both halves — the frame is the plan-telling frame

variations.cue: I will eat the bread in the morning
variations.changed: ghadan → fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ: M4's time phrases work in the future too

variations.cue: He will eat the bread and drink the milk
variations.changed: both halves turn to ya- under their own sa-: his plans, each verb marked for itself

mistake.display: ghadan sa-ākul al-khubz wa sa-tashrab al-ḥalīb
mistake.why: Meant all as "I", but the second verb slipped to ta-, "you". Each verb owns its person, and both here are I: sa-ākul … sa-ashrab — M5's lesson at the front of the word instead of the back.

sentences.usage: Two plans in one breath — the shape M10 will turn into a whole turn.
sentences.mnemonic: Two verbs, two sa-: the future is not a word you can share.

comprehensionPool.cue: I will go to work tomorrow
Will you drink the tea? (to a man)
Tomorrow I will eat the fruit
She will be busy in the afternoon
Soon he will go to the market

comprehensionPool.display: sa-ashrab al-qahwa fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ, in shāʾ Allāh
comprehensionPool.script: سأشرب القهوة في الصباح، إن شاء الله
comprehensionPool.cue: I will drink the coffee in the morning, God willing
